text:

author: hlntnr
text:
Ajeya with (as always) smart thoughts on a dynamic that's central to fights about AI risks, namely: 

Everyone would love to only act on the basis of rock-solid empirical evidence... but some serious thinkers worry we're not going to get that in time. How do we handle that??

quoted.text: I resonate with this principle from Dean Ball's post last week and AI Snake Oil's post last month. Agree freedom+tech are both usually great. I'd be pissed about limits on tech *I* like based on speculative risks *I* don't buy. But we're in a tough epistemic bind 🧵 https://t.co/cPFu4tWa4c

author: hlntnr
text:
New piece out with my colleague Zach Arnold, laying out some basic common-sense policies that people with a wide range of views on AI could get behind:

-Building govt capacity
-Better measurement
-Independent auditing
-Disclosure
-Incident tracking
-Liability

🧵: https://t.co/IgqW608ATp

author: hlntnr
text: Most interesting part of this IMO: the q of how light-touch vs onerous SB1047 will be is one of the biggest points of genuine/honest contention about it. Lessig (a top legal scholar & OG proponent of open source) calling it "remarkably light-touch" should matter for that debate.

author: hlntnr
text:

quoted.text:
The need for better AI evaluations has been a recurring theme in AI policy over the last year—from Biden’s executive order, to the UK Safety Summit.

But, why are evaluations so important, and so hard to do well? @Thomas_Woodside and @hlntnr explain ⬇️https://t.co/DwdjGdYsl0

author: hlntnr
text:
Getting to work with technical experts like @timrudner to translate their expertise for a wider audience is one of my favorite parts of my job.

This is the 5th "key concepts" paper we've written, and it's special because it's truly about Tim's specialty. Hope you enjoy!

7/8

author: hlntnr
text:
New "Key Concepts in AI Safety" just dropped 👀

If you've ever wished for a chatbot that would give a confidence score with its answers, this one's for you. 

Why is it so hard to train AI models that know when they're likely to be right, and when they might be wrong?

🧵1/8

quoted.text:
✨New Report✨

Can we create AI systems that know what they don’t know? This challenge is known as “uncertainty quantification,” and our new explainer by @timrudner and @hlntnr digs into how it works.

Check it out here ⬇️ https://t.co/LqSJPpNVIa

text:
